## The Paper

**Greener JG, Kandathil SM, Moffat L, Jones DT (2022)**

*A guide to machine learning for biologists*

Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology

DOI: [10.1038/s41580-021-00407-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41580-021-00407-0)

::: {.notes}
Review/tutorial paper aimed at biologists entering ML. Not a research paper — covers supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning, evaluation, and best practices with biological examples.
:::

---

## Pre-reading Questions

1. How do the authors categorize the landscape of ML methods — what's the "taxonomy"?
2. Which evaluation metrics matter most, and when is accuracy misleading?
3. What is overfitting, and how do you detect and prevent it?
4. Which ML methods map to which data types (images, sequences, tabular)?
5. What practical best practices can we apply in our own work?

## The ML Taxonomy

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
flowchart TD
    ML["Machine Learning"]
    ML --> SL["Supervised Learning"]
    ML --> UL["Unsupervised Learning"]
    ML --> SSL["Self-supervised Learning"]
    SL --> Class["Classification"]
    SL --> Reg["Regression"]
    SL --> CML["Classical ML<br/>Random Forest, SVM,<br/>Logistic Regression"]
    SL --> DL["Deep Learning<br/>CNN, RNN, Transformer"]
    UL --> Clust["Clustering<br/>k-means, DBSCAN"]
    UL --> DimRed["Dimensionality Reduction<br/>PCA, t-SNE, UMAP"]
    SSL --> Pretrain["Pre-training on<br/>unlabeled data"]

    style ML fill:#2a6496,color:#fff
    style SL fill:#3a7ca5,color:#fff
    style UL fill:#3a7ca5,color:#fff
    style SSL fill:#3a7ca5,color:#fff
```

::: {.notes}
Q1 answer: The paper organizes ML into supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised. Within supervised, classical ML vs deep learning.
:::

## Which Method for Which Data?

| Data Type | Examples in Our Work | Recommended Methods |
|---|---|---|
| **Tabular / clinical** | Patient variables, AST results | Random Forest, Logistic Regression, XGBoost |
| **Images** | MALDI-TOF spectra, microscopy | CNN (Convolutional Neural Networks) |
| **Sequences** | Genomic data, protein sequences | RNN → Transformer |
| **Text** | Clinical notes, literature | LLMs (Transformer-based) |
| **Mixed** | Multi-modal clinical data | Ensemble / hybrid approaches |

---

## Evaluation Metrics — Beyond Accuracy

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Why accuracy is misleading

If 99% of samples are negative:

- A model that **always says "negative"** gets **99% accuracy**
- But it's **completely useless** for detecting resistant strains

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Better metrics

| Metric | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **Precision** | Of predicted positives, how many are true? |
| **Recall** | Of actual positives, how many did we find? |
| **F1** | Harmonic mean of precision & recall |
| **AUC-ROC** | Threshold-independent quality |

:::
:::

---

## The Confusion Matrix

|  | **Predicted Positive** | **Predicted Negative** |
|---|---|---|
| **Actually Positive** | ✅ True Positive (TP) | ❌ False Negative (FN) |
| **Actually Negative** | ❌ False Positive (FP) | ✅ True Negative (TN) |

<br>

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \qquad \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$

$$F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$$

---

## Overfitting vs. Generalization

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Overfitting = Memorization

- High training accuracy
- Low test accuracy
- Model learns noise, not patterns

### Key signs

- Training loss keeps dropping
- Validation loss starts **increasing**
- Performance collapses on new data

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Prevention strategies

1. **Cross-validation** — robust estimation
2. **Regularization** — penalize complexity
3. **Early stopping** — stop before overfitting
4. **More data** — the simplest cure
5. **Simpler model** — sometimes RF beats DNN

:::
:::

## Data Handling Best Practices

### The three-way split

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 9
flowchart LR
    D["All Data"] --> Train["Training Set<br/>~60-70%<br/>Model learns"]
    D --> Val["Validation Set<br/>~15-20%<br/>Tune hyperparams"]
    D --> Test["Test Set<br/>~15-20%<br/>Final eval ONLY"]

    style D fill:#2a6496,color:#fff
    style Train fill:#27ae60,color:#fff
    style Val fill:#f39c12,color:#fff
    style Test fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff
```

### Dangers

- **Data leakage** — test info bleeds into training
- **No independent test set** — reporting validation as final results
- **Small biological datasets** — use k-fold cross-validation

---

## Simple vs. Complex Models

| Choose **Random Forest / SVM** when... | Choose **Deep Learning** when... |
|---|---|
| Small dataset (< 1000 samples) | Large dataset (> 10,000 samples) |
| Tabular / structured features | Raw images, sequences, spectra |
| Interpretability matters | Performance is the priority |
| Quick prototyping needed | Complex patterns in data |
| Features are well-defined | Features need to be learned |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb
Start simple. Only move to deep learning when simpler approaches are insufficient.
:::

---

## Where Do LLMs Fit?

Paper predates LLM explosion (ChatGPT: Nov 2022) — **not explicitly covered**.

But the building blocks are all here:

| Paper's concept | Connection to LLMs |
|---|---|
| Neural networks | LLMs are neural networks — just very large |
| RNNs | Predecessor for language — LLMs replaced these |
| Transformers (brief mention) | **The** architecture LLMs are built on |
| Self-supervised learning | How LLMs train: predict next word |
| Transfer learning | Pre-train generally, fine-tune specifically |

## Strengths & Limitations

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### ✅ Strengths

- Broad, accessible overview for biologists
- Good coverage of practical pitfalls
- Strong biological examples throughout
- Foundational vocabulary for all later sessions

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

### ⚠️ Limitations

- Pre-LLM era — misses biggest AI shift
- Limited transformer coverage
- No prompt engineering, RLHF, or agentic AI
- Some advice may need updating

:::
:::
